name: Blue Bottle — branded map beside address and weekly hours
borrow: a quiet split map-and-hours panel followed by large venue photography and nearby-location routes
why: Visitors can answer where and when before exploring the atmosphere of the place.
fit: A walk-in venue or local branch whose address and opening schedule are the primary visit-planning questions.
avoid: A destination with complex seasonal admission rules that cannot be represented by a weekly schedule alone.
slots: Venue name; linked full address; map/pin; weekly hours; local pickup/delivery route if relevant; venue photograph and caption; nearby locations.
composition: On a warm pale background, a large low-saturation map with a branded pin fills the left half. The right half centers the place name, underlined address and a vertically spaced seven-day schedule. A large environmental photograph follows, with a small location caption and related venue content below.
mobile_behavior: At 390 px the map stacks before the place identity, address and full schedule. The venue photo becomes a narrower portrait-like crop. A persistent pickup/delivery control sits at the bottom and can reduce available reading space; the hours continue below the initial capture.
rebuild: Use a structured branch record containing address, coordinates, timezone, weekly hours, holiday exceptions and service URLs. Render address and hours as accessible HTML independently of the map. Use a map provider or a properly attributed static map with a directions link. Supply a useful fallback when maps are blocked. Keep branch photography and related-location links in separate components.
assets: Licensed map output with required attribution, approved brand pin, and original exterior/interior photographs. Include an entrance-identification photo when useful. Maintain accurate branch data and a named owner for updates.
adapt: Prioritize the address and today's hours above the map on phones when speed matters. Include step-free entrance, transit or parking guidance where needed. Add date-specific exceptions and avoid showing Closed as a loading default. Keep sticky actions clear of the final schedule rows.
interaction: The settled live page exposed a linked address and a full seven-day schedule; initial loading briefly showed closed values before real hours arrived. Desktop and phone information/photo views inspected. Address destinations and pickup/delivery were not activated; map panning, geolocation, related-location navigation and holiday handling were not tested. An unsolicited newsletter overlay was dismissed without submitting data.
verification: Live desktop and 390 px phone layouts inspected and saved evidence reviewed. Editorial scores describe conversion clarity and visual impact, not measured results. No complete rebuild or accessibility audit performed. Source screenshots are study material rather than reusable client assets.

name: National Trust — date-specific visit information with facility-level opening times
borrow: a selectable visit calendar paired with opening times for individual facilities inside a practical-information disclosure
why: Visitors can distinguish which parts of a destination are open on their intended day instead of relying on one misleading global time.
fit: A destination with seasonal dates and different schedules for grounds, buildings, food, shops or activities.
avoid: A simple appointment-only service or a venue that cannot keep date-specific operational data current.
slots: Destination identity/address; opening/prices/map shortcuts; visitor-information tabs; practical section disclosures; date picker; open/closed legend; facility/time table; last-entry exceptions; planning/accessibility routes.
composition: A place introduction and landscape image precede a tabbed information area. The expanded Opening times disclosure uses a large pale panel: a ruled facility/time table occupies the left, while a month selector and calendar sit right. Operational caveats appear directly below the table. Other practical categories remain as distinct disclosures.
mobile_behavior: The information tabs form a horizontal strip. Inside the expanded section, calendar and open/closed legend move above the date-labeled facility table. The table fits the narrow width with clear row rules. Last-entry and closure notes remain next to the schedule rather than disappearing into a separate FAQ.
rebuild: Define a destination/facility calendar model with timezone, date ranges, exceptions, closed days and last-entry notes. Derive the selected date heading and table from one state source. Build a semantic calendar with accessible day labels and keyboard operation, plus a semantic table for facilities. Use disclosure buttons with expanded state. Keep the selected date visible and provide a non-calendar route for assistive technology.
assets: Original destination photography, reliable facility data and a content update process. The calendar needs accurate business rules more than decorative artwork. Maps and access documents should remain separately available.
adapt: Do not present event booking or ticket availability as equivalent to opening hours. Retain dates in accessible labels and textual headings; do not encode open/closed state only in color. Put urgent closures and access limitations before promotional copy. A simpler location can use the same table without a calendar.
interaction: Opening times disclosure opened. Selecting 7 November 2026 changed the selected day and table heading from 6 to 7 November; the coffee-shop closing time also changed. Phone layout retained the chosen date and stacked calendar above table. The initial shortcut click occurred while a cookie overlay was present, so successful shortcut scrolling is not claimed. Other tabs, month changes, booking, maps and accessibility disclosures were not exercised.
verification: Live desktop and 390 px phone layouts inspected and saved evidence reviewed. Editorial scores describe conversion clarity and visual impact, not measured results. No complete rebuild or accessibility audit performed. Source screenshots are study material rather than reusable client assets.

name: The Hoxton — curated neighborhood places with photographic discovery cards
borrow: an editorial neighborhood introduction leading into staggered place photographs with practical recommendation copy
why: The surrounding area becomes a tangible reason to choose the location, supported by specific places and onward routes.
fit: A hotel, residential development, campus or venue where the surrounding neighborhood materially influences the decision.
avoid: A local service whose visitors only need directions, or a location guide without maintained recommendations and valid destination links.
slots: Neighborhood title and introduction; place name; permissioned photo; reason to visit; contextual tip; destination URL; category/distance when available; persistent host-location conversion route.
composition: A warm cream section centers a short heading above a narrower serif introduction. Below, tall photographic place cards sit in staggered columns. A coral text face was visible on one desktop card, carrying its name, recommendation and onward action. The introduction remains visually behind the moving card composition at some scroll positions.
mobile_behavior: The centered introduction wraps into a narrow readable column. Place cards become a horizontal rail with a partial next card visible. Each visible phone card shows the image followed by name, recommendation text and a normal onward link; this makes the copy available without a hover dependency. The hotel booking action remains in the compact header.
rebuild: Model recommendations as maintained records with name, category, image, description, contextual advice and URL. Build ordinary linked cards first, then add staggered desktop placement or an optional reveal treatment. On phones use a reachable horizontal list with snap points or a simpler stacked list. Preserve full text and links for touch, keyboard and reduced-motion users.
assets: Original or licensed neighborhood photographs with consistent crops, current destination URLs and genuinely local editorial recommendations. Do not reuse source partner imagery or borrow unverified claims about a venue.
adapt: Add walking distance, transit and accessibility context where the client can substantiate it. Keep the neighborhood introduction readable instead of letting animation obstruct it. Avoid making the full card a link with an excessively long accessible name. Supply explicit carousel controls or a non-carousel list if users cannot discover all places easily.
interaction: Desktop and phone layouts inspected. A desktop card's text face was visible while the pointer was in its area, but the hover/focus trigger was not isolated or keyboard-tested. Phone text and links were visibly available below photographs. Horizontal swipe behavior and external destination navigation were not exercised. Newsletter/cookie overlays were dismissed without signup; no room search or booking was submitted.
verification: Live desktop and 390 px phone layouts inspected and saved evidence reviewed. Editorial scores describe conversion clarity and visual impact, not measured results. No complete rebuild or accessibility audit performed. Source screenshots are study material rather than reusable client assets.

name: Nielsen Norman Group — educational article with summary, contents and dense tables
borrow: a prominent summary and author/date block above a readable essay, with contents navigation and related resources beside the body
why: Readers can judge relevance quickly and navigate substantial explanatory material without losing the author's context.
fit: An evergreen educational article with headings, structured lists, supporting links and potentially dense comparison tables.
avoid: A primarily photographic narrative or an extremely short announcement where a contents mechanism adds unnecessary complexity.
slots: Article title; linked author and portrait; publication date; summary; body headings/paragraphs/lists; contents links; tables; related courses/topics; sharing route.
composition: A bold sans-serif title and compact author/date row lead into a large serif summary marked by a light vertical rule. The main reading column uses generous line height and paragraph spacing. A narrower right rail presents related learning and topic routes. Body tables are ruled and retain row/column relationships.
mobile_behavior: The title, author and summary stack at full content width. The right rail leaves the initial reading view. While scrolled within a later section, an In This Article strip stays at the top and displays the current section with a disclosure cue. The comparison table fits narrow columns but wraps into tall, dense cells.
rebuild: Use a structured article body supporting headings, ordered/unordered lists, callouts and semantic tables. Generate contents anchors from stable heading IDs. Keep author metadata and summary separate from body content. Use a constrained reading measure, fluid type and an optional desktop related-content rail. Provide an accessible mobile contents disclosure and offset anchored headings for sticky controls.
assets: Approved author portrait, reliable author/date metadata and original educational diagrams when needed. Use HTML for tables and summaries so text remains selectable and accessible. The source essay and tables are reference content, not copy to republish.
adapt: Keep the summary short enough to earn its prominent treatment. For wide tables, choose horizontal overflow with persistent headers or a deliberate alternative instead of crushing columns. Distinguish publication and updated dates when both exist. Ensure related commercial content stays secondary to reading.
interaction: Article header, body/table and phone layout inspected. Selecting a contents link was attempted while a privacy notice appeared, so direct contents-jump behavior is not claimed. Manual scrolling exposed the phone current-section contents strip. Its disclosure, sharing, related resources and full keyboard behavior were not tested. Privacy notice dismissed without form submission.
verification: Live desktop and 390 px phone layouts inspected and saved evidence reviewed. Editorial scores describe conversion clarity and visual impact, not measured results. No complete rebuild or accessibility audit performed. Source screenshots are study material rather than reusable client assets.

name: Stripe — technical article with an author rail and inline demonstration
borrow: an offset reading column with a separate author-expertise rail, clear section headings and an inline demonstration poster
why: The article presents its author and practical explanation without requiring a large decorative hero before readers reach useful content.
fit: A product explanation or expert announcement with substantive text, a demonstration and a clear next information route.
avoid: A deeply nested reference manual or a story whose meaning depends on large immersive photography.
slots: Publication/category breadcrumb; title; date; author name/portrait/role; introductory paragraphs; section headings; demonstration poster/video; structured examples; documentation routes; optional post-article subscription.
composition: A light ruled page grid aligns a large headline and date over the main reading column, offset to the right. The author portrait, name and role occupy a smaller left rail at the beginning of the body. Inline links use a distinct accent. A wide colored video poster interrupts the text at the relevant explanation point.
mobile_behavior: The title, date and author block move into one reading column before the body. Sections retain clear heading scale and paragraph rhythm. The inline media shrinks to the content width with a visible play control and stays after its explanatory text. The desktop side-rail spacing is removed.
rebuild: Store author expertise, date, category and body as separate fields. Use a desktop grid with a constrained reading column and a metadata rail, then flatten to logical mobile order. Support headings, lists and media figures as reusable body blocks. Load a poster first, reserve aspect ratio and only initialize video when requested. Add captions/transcript and a useful static fallback.
assets: Client-approved author portrait/role, original product demonstration and a purpose-made poster that remains understandable at phone width. Keep sample data synthetic and hide private account information. Do not reuse source pricing, product claims or example prompts as client content.
adapt: Move documentation or action links to the point where the reader can use them. Add a contents list only when length warrants it. Prefer 60–75-character reading measures rather than reproducing overly wide text lines. Keep newsletter and recruiting prompts after the article rather than inside its core explanation.
interaction: Desktop and phone article header/body inspected; media poster and play control were visible. Video playback, transcript controls and documentation routes were not activated. No connection, subscription or other form action was submitted. Product/API claims were not independently verified; this record documents the presentation and content structure.
verification: Live desktop and 390 px phone layouts inspected and saved evidence reviewed. Editorial scores describe conversion clarity and visual impact, not measured results. No complete rebuild or accessibility audit performed. Source screenshots are study material rather than reusable client assets.

name: Figma Shortcut — illustrated research article with captioned evidence pairs
borrow: a bold colored article lead followed by a narrower reading column and paired visual evidence with separate explanatory captions
why: The visual system gives a technical story character while figures explain specific points rather than acting as decoration.
fit: An original research or thought-leadership article with substantive evidence and a budget for editorial visual assets.
avoid: A thin post with generic artwork, or a client unable to supply accurate examples and meaningful figure captions.
slots: Publication masthead; date; large title; author/role; topic tags; lead illustration; standfirst; art credit; body headings/links; comparison figures and captions; diagrams; share controls.
composition: A pale yellow surface extends from the oversized headline into the article. Author information and outlined tags form a metadata row before a wide illustration. The body narrows to a reading column; selected figures extend wider. A before/after pair uses two equal images, each with its own caption describing the input and observed output.
mobile_behavior: The title becomes a large multi-line block; author/role and tags wrap below it. The lead illustration crops into the content width. Body text stays in one column, and the evidence pair stacks vertically with each caption following its corresponding image. This preserves association at the cost of simultaneous side-by-side comparison.
rebuild: Define article blocks for prose, linked headings, full-width artwork, standard figures, paired figures and diagrams. Use figure/figcaption semantics and meaningful alt text that complements captions. Give section headings stable anchors. Keep wide visual blocks on a separate grid track from prose, with a single-column phone order. Reserve media dimensions to prevent anchor drift.
assets: Original commissioned editorial illustration with artist credit, client-owned screenshots, and diagrams produced from accurate evidence. Ensure figure text is legible at the intended crop. Publish accessible text equivalents for charts or complex pipeline drawings; do not reuse the source illustrations or experimental claims.
adapt: Use a quieter surface or neutral body region if a long colored page harms reading comfort. Caption the difference a reader should inspect; avoid unsupported success claims. For comparison tasks needing simultaneous views on phones, offer an accessible alternate arrangement or a concise annotated composite.
interaction: The heading link Teaching a model to edit in Figma updated the URL to its matching fragment, establishing a linkable section route. Desktop side-by-side and phone stacked comparison figures inspected. Share actions, tag overflow, lightbox behavior and full keyboard traversal were not exercised. No newsletter or social-sharing action was submitted.
verification: Live desktop and 390 px phone layouts inspected and saved evidence reviewed. Editorial scores describe conversion clarity and visual impact, not measured results. No complete rebuild or accessibility audit performed. Source screenshots are study material rather than reusable client assets.
